articles.title: Federal Reserve Faces Challenge as Americans Accept Higher Prices as Norm
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve is concerned that consumers and businesses are accepting higher prices as the new normal, making it harder to control inflation.
articles.content: The Federal Reserve's efforts to control inflation are facing a new challenge: Americans' growing acceptance of higher prices as the norm. According to Fed Governor Chris Waller, many people now see 3% inflation as the standard rate, rather than an exception. This shift in psychology is concerning for the central bank, which has been trying to keep inflation within its 2% target for years. The latest consumer price index data shows that prices are rising faster than expected, and this trend is not limited to areas affected by higher energy costs or tariffs. In fact, core services, a key indicator of underlying inflation, are also seeing significant increases. In a recent interview with CNBC, Waller acknowledged that businesses are starting to factor 3% price hikes into their plans, rather than treating them as temporary. He cited an example of someone who passed on a 3% increase to consumers because they assumed it was the maximum amount they would accept. The problem, according to Waller, is that when households and businesses expect prices to keep rising, they set wages and prices accordingly, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of inflation. This is exactly what the Fed wants to avoid, especially after more than five years above its 2% target. The central bank's efforts to curb inflation are being hindered by a growing perception that higher prices have become the new normal. This mindset is causing concern for Fed officials, who believe it may lead consumers and businesses to accept and even pass on increased costs. To combat this trend, Waller suggests that the Fed needs to be more proactive in its rate hikes. He advocates for a more aggressive approach, potentially including a larger-than-usual half-point increase at the upcoming December meeting. A significant hike of this nature would raise the benchmark interest rate to between 4.25% and 4.5%, up from the current range of 3.75% to 4%. This move would be a departure from the Fed's recent approach, which saw it raise rates for the first time in over three years in September before holding steady in October. Despite Waller's push for more aggressive action, market expectations remain cautious. Futures are currently pricing in a quarter-point hike in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. However, some officials believe that even this modest increase could be effective if accompanied by clear signals of further hikes in the months ahead. The lingering effects of tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump have added complexity to the economic situation. Instead of being implemented all at once, the levies were delayed due to ongoing negotiations and legal challenges that repeatedly put them on and off again. As a result, businesses did not immediately pass on the full cost of tariffs but instead spread it out over time. This gradual increase in costs has likely contributed to the inflationary pressures that are now being felt. The cumulative effect is weighing heavily on consumer attitudes. The ongoing tensions with Iran have also had an impact on oil prices, which remain volatile despite having receded from their recent highs. Whenever fighting in the Persian Gulf escalates, oil prices spike, further contributing to the economic uncertainty. Minutes from the Fed's October meeting suggest that inflation expectations may be becoming unmoored after five years of elevated inflation. This is a concern for policymakers who are trying to anchor long-term inflation expectations at a manageable level. Fed Governor Lisa Cook echoed Waller's concerns about consumer psychology in her explanation of her dissenting vote on interest rate hikes. She emphasized the need to tackle inflation, which has been above target for over five and a half years, posing an increasing risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward. The recent monetary policy decisions by the Federal Reserve are being closely watched as inflation continues to pose a challenge. New York Fed President John Williams expressed a cautious stance, stating that there's no need for "dramatic action" in addressing the issue. He pointed out that the gradual approach taken in recent months has been effective so far. Williams also highlighted the resilience of the economy and the solidity of the labor market. The reality is that businesses are taking advantage of this stability to pass on higher prices, making it more difficult for inflation to decrease. As a result, some policymakers believe that multiple rate hikes may be necessary to bring inflation back under control.
